items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the decline in the population of remote rural areas, mainly through out-migration of young people”.
items.answer: Rural depopulation

items.stem: Explain the causes of rural depopulation in remote areas of HICs.
items.answer: Mechanisation reduces farm jobs; few alternative jobs; young people leave for education and work; services close as thresholds fall; poor transport; isolation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause [4]

items.stem: Explain how rural settlements near large cities have changed.
items.answer: Growth of new housing for commuters; rising house prices; change from farming to service and commuter populations; increased traffic; some services (shops) close as people shop in cities, others (cafés, gastropubs) open.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per change [4]

items.stem: Village C lies 101 km from a major city. In 2001 it had 2 931 residents, 17% aged 65+, and 10 services; in 2021 it had 2 294 residents, 29% aged 65+, and 4 services. Suggest two problems the changes may cause for young local people.
items.answer: Lack of jobs, schools and transport; isolation; need to leave for education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Village C lies 13 km from a major city. In 2001 it had 1 575 residents, 16% aged 65+, and 11 services; in 2021 it had 2 237 residents, 21% aged 65+, and 9 services. (a) Suggest whether the village is experiencing counter-urbanisation or rural depopulation. Use the data. (b) Suggest two problems the changes may cause for young local people.
items.answer: (a) Counter-urbanisation: population growth close to a city, likely commuters and retirees moving in. (b) Rising house prices; competition for housing; few local jobs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark process; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Grace argues that rural areas in HICs face more problems from population growth than from population decline. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to house prices and ageing.
items.answer: For: Accessible villages face rising house prices, loss of character, traffic, conflict between newcomers and locals and pressure on schools and roads. Against: Remote areas (Scottish Highlands, rural Japan, rural Spain) face ageing, closure of schools and shops, abandoned homes and declining services. Conclusion: Both are significant; decline creates more severe long-term problems for remote areas, while growth creates manageable but contested pressures near cities.

items.stem: Explain the “cycle of decline” in remote rural areas.
items.answer: Out-migration of young adults reduces population and births; services lose thresholds and close; fewer jobs and services encourage further out-migration; the population ages.

items.stem: Grace argues that lack of access to land is the main cause of rural poverty in LICs. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Landlessness and tiny plots limit food production (Bangladesh, Bihar); insecure tenure discourages investment; land grabs displace farmers. Against: Lack of infrastructure, markets, credit, education and health care; climate shocks and conflict; low crop prices; limited non-farm employment. items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “Rural areas in HICs have higher proportions of elderly people than cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the causes of rural depopulation in remote areas of HICs.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Young adults leave and retired people move in, raising the median age. (b) Mechanisation reduces farm jobs; few alternative jobs; young people leave for education and work; services close as thresholds fall; poor transport; isolation.

items.answer: (a) Not correct. Accessible rural areas near cities are growing through counter-urbanisation; remote areas may decline. (b) Mechanisation reduces farm jobs; few alternative jobs; young people leave for education and work; services close as thresholds fall; poor transport; isolation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per cause [4]

items.stem: Village C lies 8 km from a major city. In 2001 it had 2 882 residents, 20% aged 65+, and 12 services; in 2021 it had 3 780 residents, 24% aged 65+, and 15 services. (a) Suggest whether the village is experiencing counter-urbanisation or rural depopulation. Use the data. (b) Explain the change in the number of services.
items.answer: (a) Counter-urbanisation: population growth close to a city, likely commuters and retirees moving in. (b) Growth in population may support some services, but commuters shop in the city, so the change is small.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that rural areas in HICs face more problems from population growth than from population decline?
items.answer: For: Accessible villages face rising house prices, loss of character, traffic, conflict between newcomers and locals and pressure on schools and roads. Against: Remote areas (Scottish Highlands, rural Japan, rural Spain) face ageing, closure of schools and shops, abandoned homes and declining services. Conclusion: Both are significant; decline creates more severe long-term problems for remote areas, while growth creates manageable but contested pressures near cities.

items.stem: Assess the view that lack of access to land is the main cause of rural poverty in LICs. In your answer you may refer to services and land tenure.
items.answer: For: Landlessness and tiny plots limit food production (Bangladesh, Bihar); insecure tenure discourages investment; land grabs displace farmers. Against: Lack of infrastructure, markets, credit, education and health care; climate shocks and conflict; low crop prices; limited non-farm employment. Conclusion: Access to land is fundamental, but without infrastructure, credit and services land alone does not lift households out of poverty.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “green belt”?
options: A zone of protected open land around a city where development is strictly controlled.
The development of new, non-farming economic activities in rural areas, such as tourism or crafts.
Housing provided at below market price or rent for people on lower incomes.
A planning approach that improves farming, infrastructure, services and employment together.
items.answer: A zone of protected open land around a city where development is strictly controlled.
items.markingKey: Green belt: a zone of protected open land around a city where development is strictly controlled. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Rural diversification can reduce dependence on farming.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Green belts have stopped all development around cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Tourism, crafts and services provide additional incomes. (b) Not correct. Development jumps beyond the green belt and some land is released; commuting increases.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Rural diversification can reduce dependence on farming.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how rural development schemes in LICs can reduce rural-urban migration.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Tourism, crafts and services provide additional incomes. (b) Creating rural jobs (MGNREGA), improving roads, water, electricity, schools and clinics, credit for farmers; reducing push factors.

items.stem: Planners must choose one village as a key settlement for a new health centre and secondary school. Each village is scored 1-5 against four criteria, which are weighted: population (weight 3), road access (weight 3), existing services (weight 3), land available (weight 3). Scores: Village P: 5, 4, 3, 5; Village Q: 5, 2, 5, 3; Village R: 3, 2, 1, 3. Suggest two limitations of using a weighted matrix to make this decision.
items.answer: Weights and scores are subjective; important factors (e.g. community views, environmental impact) may be left out; small differences may not be meaningful.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Rural planning is more effective in HICs than in LICs.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: HICs have strong planning systems (green belts, national parks, key settlement policies) and funding for services. Against: HIC planning has not solved housing affordability or service decline; LIC schemes such as MGNREGA and Bangladesh’s rural electrification have transformed millions of lives. Conclusion: Planning capacity is greater in HICs, but the scale of improvement achieved by some LIC rural programmes is greater.
